# Dantabhūmi Sutta (MN 125 (PTS MN iii 128))

**ID:** MN 125 (PTS MN iii 128)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Dantabhūmi Sutta  
**Title (English, from literature):** The Level of the Tamed  
**PTS:** MN iii 128  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul2.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul2.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dantabhūmi Sutta* ("The Level of the Tamed", MN 125 / PTS MN iii 128) is the 125th discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*. The narrative opens when Prince Jayasena visits the novice Aciravata to ask whether an ardent, undistracted, and resolute monk can attain one-pointedness of mind (*cittassa ekaggatā*) [Norman 1983; Shulman 2014]. When Aciravata's explanation fails to convince the prince—who maintains that someone immersed in sensual pleasures cannot realize such peace—the novice reports the exchange to the Buddha [Norman 1983; Hazra 1994]. The Buddha explains that Prince Jayasena, accustomed to the pleasures of worldly life, could not see what is known only through renunciation, and shows how Aciravata could have answered by employing similes drawn from the training and taming of wild elephants, a domain with which the prince was familiar [Hazra 1994; Anālayo 2003].

**Sources**

- [Norman 1983] K. R. Norman, Pali Literature (1983) — Identifies the interlocutors (Prince Jayasena and the novice Aciravata) and setting.
- [Shulman 2014] Eviatar Shulman, Rethinking the Buddha: Early Buddhist Philosophy as Meditative Perception (2014) — Details Jayasena's opening question on one-pointedness of mind and cites Anālayo's 2006 comparative study.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pali Language and Literature (1994) — Summarizes the Buddha's discourse on renunciation versus worldly enjoyment.
- [Shonin et al. 2015] Edo Shonin, William Van Gordon, and Nirbhay N. Singh, eds., Buddhist Foundations of Mindfulness (2015) — Notes the gradual path structure shared with MN 27 and MN 51.
- [Anālayo 2003] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Satipaṭṭhāna: The Direct Path to Realization (2003) — Explains the elephant simile for satipaṭṭhāna and the transitional thought-free stage before absorption.
- [Polak 2011] Grzegorz Polak, Reexamining Jhana: Towards a Critical Reconstruction of Early Buddhist Soteriology (2011) — Quotes the Pali passage regarding contemplating the body without generating discursive thoughts.
- [Bibliogr. Transl. 2015] Marcus Bingenheimer, Bibliography of Translations of Chinese Buddhist Texts (2015) — Records Anālayo's translation of the Chinese version of MN 125.
